Schema-Validating .env

config/env.js's manual PORT check said Zod was coming eventually. It only ever meant this.

config/env.js has had its own manual validation since Lesson 1 — a plain if (!process.env.PORT || Number.isNaN(port)) check, with a comment alongside it: "real schema-based validation (Zod) arrives in Week 3." That line was talking about req.body/req.params at the time, but the same reasoning applies just as well to process.env: it's untyped data from outside this program's control (an .env file, or whatever the shell happens to export), which is exactly what a schema is for — checking, and this lesson's .default(...)/coercion (earlier topic), defaulting, before anything downstream trusts it.

// Figure 3.18: config, checked with the same tool as a request body (src/config/env.js)
import 'dotenv/config';
import { z } from 'zod';

const envSchema = z.object({
  PORT: z.coerce.number().int().positive(),
  DATABASE_URL: z.string().min(1, 'DATABASE_URL is required'),
});

const result = envSchema.safeParse(process.env);

if (!result.success) {
  const problems = result.error.issues
    .map((issue) => `${issue.path.join('.')}: ${issue.message}`)
    .join('; ');
  throw new Error(`Invalid environment configuration — ${problems}`);
}

export default result.data;

Nothing here is new syntax — z.object, z.coerce.number(), safeParse, .error.issues are all exactly what validate.js already uses against req.body. What's different is when this runs: once, at import time, when server.js first loads env.js — not per-request. A malformed .env (a non-numeric PORT, a missing DATABASE_URL) now throws immediately on startup, with every problem named at once, instead of the app starting successfully and failing confusingly later the first time something actually tries to use the bad value. export default result.data is also the payoff of that early check: everything downstream that imports env.js gets back already-validated, already-coerced values — a real number for PORT, guaranteed.
